title: Sex, Spies and Silicon Valley: OpenAI Warns Staff About "Honey Pots"
source_used: New York Post (relaying the Wall Street Journal)
key_facts: The Wall Street Journal reported, citing unnamed sources, that OpenAI has been warning employees about foreign spies who may try to seduce them to steal company secrets ('honey pot' schemes).
The report cited a stranger who approached an OpenAI employee with a child at a San Francisco playground and steered the talk to the employee's work; the stranger was a spy, according to the Journal.
OpenAI training warns of sex, bribes and eavesdropping in places such as cafes, and advises screen protectors in public, wiping whiteboards after meetings and avoiding logo clothing.
Anthropic and Google have reportedly given similar warnings to staff.
The Post says the risk took on fresh urgency after a Saudi engineer was arrested the previous Friday and charged with using a device to intercept oral communications.
The Justice Department said OpenAI found a recording device in a USB port behind a television in an executive conference room in one of its San Francisco buildings, concealed in toilet paper.
The man faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine; the Post asked OpenAI for comment.
quote_evidence: OpenAI has been warning employees to beware of foreign spies who could try to seduce them in order to steal company secrets, according to a bombshell report.
Other companies in the high-stakes AI race, including Anthropic and Google, have reportedly given similar warnings to their employees.
The Post has reached out to OpenAI for comment.
why_it_matters_hint: AI firms are treating spying on staff as a real threat, after a charged case of a hidden listening device.
event_date: WSJ report 15 Oct 2026; arrest on Friday 9 Oct 2026 (per the Post)
notes: NDTV (pool link) returned an access-denied page; read the New York Post, which relays the Wall Street Journal (reported 15 Oct). The WSJ article was not read; a WSJ page titled 'AI Companies Play Cat-and-Mouse With Secret-Stealing Spies' (wsj.com/tech/ai/ai-companies-play-cat-and-mouse-with-secret-stealing-spies-160eec6b) looks like the original, but the match is unconfirmed.
